title: Jeremiah 17:1–11
context: The LORD speaks of Judah's sin as engraved on the tablet of the heart and on the altars. He warns of plunder and exile. Then comes a saying set in poetic form: the man who trusts in man is cursed and like a desert shrub, while the man who trusts in the LORD is blessed and like a tree planted by water, which closely resembles Psalm 1:3. The passage declares that the heart is deceitful above all things, and the LORD answers that he searches the mind and tests the heart. A proverb about a partridge closes the section, warning about unjust riches.

verses.text: “The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, and with the point of a diamond. It is engraved on the tablet of their heart, and on the horns of your altars.
verses.arminianNotes: "The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, and with the point of a diamond." Arminian readers see sin deeply carved into the people's lives, written "on the tablet of their heart."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the striking image: sin is engraved where God's law should be written. They compare the promise of 31:33, while pointing to the site’s existing boxes at Deuteronomy 10:16 and Hebrews 8:10 rather than opening a new debate here.

verses.text: Even their children remember their altars and their Asherah poles by the green trees on the high hills.
verses.arminianNotes: "Even their children remember their altars and their Asherah poles." Arminian readers see idolatry passed down to the next generation, so that children grow up familiar with false worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note how sin spreads through a whole community. The altars "by the green trees on the high hills" are part of the culture the children inherit.

verses.text: My mountain in the field, I will give your substance and all your treasures for a plunder, and your high places, because of sin, throughout all your borders.
verses.arminianNotes: "My mountain in the field, I will give your substance and all your treasures for a plunder." Arminian readers see the LORD warning that Judah's wealth and high places will be lost because of sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the phrase "My mountain in the field" is difficult and is read in different ways, though it likely refers to Jerusalem. The point is that judgment will reach everything Judah values.

verses.text: You, even of yourself, will discontinue from your heritage that I gave you. I will cause you to serve your enemies in the land which you don’t know, for you have kindled a fire in my anger which will burn forever.”
verses.arminianNotes: "You, even of yourself, will discontinue from your heritage that I gave you." Arminian readers see Judah's loss of the land as the result of its own choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the heritage was the LORD's gift, and the people's sin "kindled a fire in my anger." Both traditions agree that the loss is just and self-inflicted.

verses.text: The LORD says: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, relies on strength of flesh, and whose heart departs from the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: "Cursed is the man who trusts in man." Arminian readers see a choice set before every person: whether to rely on human strength or on the LORD. The curse falls on the one "whose heart departs from the LORD."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that trust in man is tied to a heart turning from God. They compare Proverbs 28:26: "One who trusts in himself is a fool." Both traditions treat this warning as shared ground.

verses.text: For he will be like a bush in the desert, and will not see when good comes, but will inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, an uninhabited salt land.
verses.arminianNotes: "For he will be like a bush in the desert." Arminian readers see the barren life of the one who trusts in man, who "will not see when good comes" and dwells in a salt land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the contrast with the tree of verse 8. Life without trust in God is dry and fruitless. The image is vivid and needs no forced theological contrast.

verses.text: “Blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD, and whose confidence is in the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: "Blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD." Arminian readers see the invitation to trust the LORD, whose confidence brings blessing. Trust is the faithful response God calls for.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the emphasis on confidence "in the LORD," not in one's own faithfulness. They compare Psalm 2:12: "Blessed are all those who take refuge in him." Both traditions see this as shared ground.

verses.text: For he will be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and will not fear when heat comes, but its leaf will be green, and will not be concerned in the year of drought. It won’t cease from yielding fruit.
verses.arminianNotes: "For he will be as a tree planted by the waters." Arminian readers see the one who trusts the LORD remaining fruitful even "in the year of drought." Trust sustains through hard times.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note how closely this resembles Psalm 1:3, "like a tree planted by the streams of water." They name the parallel and note that Jeremiah adds the heat and drought the tree endures.

verses.text: The heart is deceitful above all things and it is exceedingly corrupt. Who can know it?
verses.arminianNotes: "The heart is deceitful above all things and it is exceedingly corrupt." Arminian readers see a sober picture of human sinfulness, while holding that God's grace can still reach and renew the heart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read this as strong testimony to the heart's corruption. The site’s existing box at Genesis 6:5 already treats the shared conviction and the fork over inability, so this verse does not open a new one.

verses.text: “I, the LORD, search the mind. I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.”
verses.arminianNotes: "I, the LORD, search the mind." Arminian readers see the LORD answering the question "Who can know it?" He tests the heart to give each person "according to his ways."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers compare 1 Samuel 16:7, "the LORD looks at the heart," and Romans 2:6. God alone truly knows the heart, and his judgment is fully just. Both traditions treat this as shared ground.

verses.text: As the partridge that sits on eggs which she has not laid, so is he who gets riches, and not by right. In the middle of his days, they will leave him. At his end, he will be a fool.
verses.arminianNotes: "As the partridge that sits on eggs which she has not laid." Arminian readers see a warning about gaining wealth unjustly: such riches will leave a person "In the middle of his days."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the image is proverbial and its natural-history details need not be pressed. The point is plain: the one who gets riches "not by right" will prove a fool at the end.
